statement: A set $B$ of elements of a vector space $V$ over a field $F$ is a basis if every element of $V$ can be written in a unique way as a finite linear combination of elements of $B$: $\mathbf{v} = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i \mathbf{b}_i$ with $\mathbf{b}_i \in B$ and $\lambda_i \in F$. Equivalently, $B$ is a linearly independent spanning set of $V$. The supplied sources contain no derivation of basis, as it is an elementary definition.

symbols.meaning: coordinate/coefficient of vector v with respect to basis vector b_i
number of vectors in a finite basis, or dimension of V

properties.property: A set $B$ is a basis of $V$ if and only if its elements are linearly independent and every element of $V$ is a linear combination of elements of $B$ (a linearly independent spanning set).
properties.why: uniqueness of finite linear combination representations is equivalent to linear independence combined with the spanning property

properties.property: All bases of a vector space $V$ have the same cardinality, which is defined as the dimension of $V$.
properties.why: follows from the Steinitz exchange lemma

properties.property: A generating set $S$ of $V$ is a basis if and only if it is minimal (no proper subset of $S$ is also a generating set of $V$).
properties.why: removing any vector from a basis destroys the spanning property due to linear independence

properties.property: A linearly independent set $L$ is a basis if and only if it is maximal (it is not a proper subset of any linearly independent set).
properties.why: any vector not in the span would allow extending the linearly independent set, so maximality implies spanning

properties.property: In a vector space of dimension $n$, a subset of $n$ elements is a basis if and only if it is linearly independent, or equivalently if and only if it is a spanning set.
properties.why: for a set whose cardinality matches the dimension, linear independence and spanning are equivalent

properties.property: An ordered basis $(\mathbf{b}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_n)$ of $V$ over $F$ defines a linear isomorphism $\varphi: F^n \to V$ given by $(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n) \mapsto \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i \mathbf{b}_i$, mapping the canonical basis $\mathbf{e}_i$ of $F^n$ to $\mathbf{b}_i$.
properties.why: every vector is uniquely determined by its coordinates in $F^n$

assumptions.assumption: Linear combinations of basis elements must be finite sums.
assumptions.breaks_when: Infinite linear combinations are considered in spaces equipped with topology (such as Fourier series, orthogonal bases in Hilbert spaces, or Schauder bases in Banach spaces).
Scalars belong to a general ring $R$ rather than a field, giving a module where bases may not exist (non-free modules).

assumptions.assumption: Every vector space has a basis.
assumptions.breaks_when: In infinite-dimensional vector spaces without assuming the Axiom of Choice or the ultrafilter lemma.

failure_modes.signature: A vector has multiple distinct coordinate representations, or the zero vector is expressed as a non-trivial linear combination.
failure_modes.cause: The candidate set of vectors is linearly dependent.

failure_modes.signature: Certain vectors in $V$ cannot be expressed as a linear combination of the candidate set.
failure_modes.cause: The candidate set fails to generate/span $V$.

failure_modes.mode: Absence of a basis in modules
failure_modes.signature: No linearly independent generating set exists for the algebraic structure.
failure_modes.cause: The algebraic structure is a module over a ring rather than a vector space over a field (e.g., non-free abelian groups with torsion).

failure_modes.mode: Countability breakdown in complete infinite-dimensional normed spaces
failure_modes.signature: Countable sets cannot generate the space via finite linear combinations.
failure_modes.cause: By the Baire category theorem, any Hamel basis of an infinite-dimensional Banach space is necessarily uncountable.
